When God told him to destroy Amalek utterly, he spared the king and the best of the sheep and called it worship. He had years of clear words from God and he treated each one as optional, a suggestion he could improve upon. And now, when the army of the Philistines is on the hill and Saul finally, frantically wants to hear, the God he ignored when His voice was easy to hear has stopped making it easy.

I am afraid of this passage because I recognize the pattern in myself. I treat conviction as negotiable when obeying is costly. I hear the small clear thing God says and I file it for later, I improve on it, I obey the part that does not hurt. And the danger is not that God strikes me down for it. The danger is subtler and worse. The danger is that I dull my own hearing, that I train myself to mistake His voice for one option among many, until the day I genuinely need to hear Him and find I have unlearned how. Silence is not always God leaving. Sometimes it is God honoring the years I spent not listening.

**The King Who Asked the Dead**

So Saul does the unthinkable. The man who himself drove the mediums and the wizards out of the land disguises himself, travels by night to Endor, and asks a woman to bring up the dead. He breaks his own law to consult the very thing he condemned, because a man who will not have God on God's terms will eventually take counsel from anywhere. And Samuel comes up, and Samuel has not softened in death. "Wherefore then dost thou ask of me, seeing the Lord is departed from thee, and is become thine enemy?" (1 Samuel 28:16). Then the verdict: tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. The army of Israel given into the hand of the Philistines. Saul falls full length on the ground, no strength left in him, because there was no bread in him all that day and night. The king of Israel collapses in a witch's house, hearing his own doom from a dead prophet, having gone everywhere except back to obedience.

We are tempted by Endor more than we admit. When God is silent we do not always wait. We go to the horoscope, the second opinion that tells us what we want, the counselor we choose because we know what he will say, the voice that is not God but is available. We will take counsel from the dead before we will repent before the living God, because repentance is the one door Saul never tried and we so often will not try either.

There is a King who also faced a silence, who cried out and for a terrible span heard nothing. "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me." But His silence was not the wages of His own disobedience. It was the wages of ours. The greater David went into the dark where God does not answer, the abandonment Saul earned, and He took it though He had not earned it, so that we who deserve the silence might be answered forever. Because Christ was forsaken, the prayers of His people are heard.

The time to hear God is while He is still speaking, while obeying still costs only your pride.

Silence from God is its own verdict.

You can come back from a long trip carrying gifts and find the house gone. That is what waited for David at Ziklag. He and his six hundred men marched three days home, and they came over the last rise expecting their wives, their children, their tents, and they saw smoke. The Amalekites had come while the men were away, burned the city with fire, and carried off every woman and child, taking none of them down but driving them all into captivity.

"Then David and the people that were with him lifted up their voice and wept, until they had no more power to weep" (1 Samuel 30:4). Grown men, hardened warriors, weeping on the ground until the weeping wore out. And then it got worse, because grief looks for somewhere to land. The men began to speak of stoning David. Every man bitter for his sons and daughters, and the cheapest comfort of a wrecked people is to find someone to blame. David had lost his own two wives in the same fire. He stood alone, the leader everyone wanted dead, in the ashes of everything.

**The Sentence That Turns the Story**

Then comes the verse the whole chapter hinges on. "But David encouraged himself in the Lord his God" (1 Samuel 30:6). Not in his men, who wanted to kill him. Not in his circumstances, which were ash. Not in himself, who had brought them all to Philistine country by fear in the first place. In the Lord his God. After a year and four months of silence at Ziklag, after living the double life of deception, David turns at last back to the One he had stopped consulting, and the first thing he does is the thing he had not done in a long time. He inquires of the Lord.

I need to be honest about how rare this is in me. When the bottom drops out, my reflexes are anything but God. I strengthen myself in being right, in being a victim, in the sympathy of others, in plans, in scrolling, in anything that fills the silence. To strengthen yourself in the Lord is not a feeling that descends on you. It is a thing David did, a verb, a deliberate turning of the soul to God when every nerve wants to turn somewhere closer. He asked for the priest and the ephod. "Shall I pursue after this troop? shall I overtake them?" And God answered, the silence finally broken: "Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all" (1 Samuel 30:8). The man who stopped asking is asking again, and heaven speaks.

**Two Kings, Two Directions**

Hold these chapters side by side, because the Bible sets them there on purpose. While David is at Ziklag strengthening himself in his God, inquiring, pursuing, and recovering all, Saul is on the other side of the country moving the opposite direction, toward Gilboa, toward the medium, toward the end. Two anointed men. Two responses to ruin. One turns to God in the ashes and is raised up. One turns from God in his fear and falls on his sword. The difference between them is not that one sinned and one did not. David's fear put Ziklag in danger. The difference is where each man turned when everything burned. Saul, abandoned, sought the dead. David, abandoned, sought the living God. And God met the one who came back.

David pursues, finds an Egyptian slave left to die in a field, revives him, and is led to the Amalekite camp. He strikes them, recovers everything, every wife, every child, every flock. "David recovered all" (1 Samuel 30:18-19). The verdict God spoke at the ephod came true to the last child.

We will all stand on a burned rise someday, looking at the smoke of something we cannot get back. And in that moment the temptation is to strengthen ourselves in our grievance, to find the man to stone, to sink. But there is another move, the harder one, the one David made. Turn to the Lord your God when there is nothing else to turn to.

There is a greater David who came to His own Ziklag, to a tomb, to a Friday where everything He loved was carried into captivity by the last enemy. And on the third day He did not merely strengthen Himself, He rose, and He recovered all, every son and daughter the enemy had stolen, leaving none of them behind. The empty tomb is the ephod's word made flesh. Without fail, recover all.

When the city is ash, do not look for someone to blame. Look up.

Strengthen yourself in your God.

There is a wall in Beth-shan, and on it, in the morning, the people of the town would have seen the body of a king. Not a stranger's body. The body of Saul, the tall one, the one the people had demanded when they told Samuel to give them a king like the nations had. The head that the oil had been poured on, the shoulders that had stood higher than any man in Israel, fastened to a pagan wall like a trophy. This is where the cry "give us a king" finally led.

The battle on Mount Gilboa went against Israel. The Philistines followed hard after Saul and his sons, and they killed Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchishua. The archers found Saul, and he was sore wounded. He asked his armorbearer to run him through so the uncircumcised would not abuse him, and the armorbearer would not, and so Saul fell on his own sword. "So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together" (1 Samuel 31:6). The whole house gone in an afternoon. The next day the Philistines found the bodies, cut off Saul's head, stripped his armor, put it in the house of their idols, and nailed his body to the wall.

**The King the People Demanded**

We should remember how Saul began before we look at how he ended, because the ending is the seed grown up. Israel had asked for a king to be like everyone else, to fight their battles, to make them feel secure the way the nations felt secure. God had warned them what such a king would take and they wanted him anyway. Saul was the answer to a prayer that should never have been prayed in that form, a king chosen for his height and his look, a king after the people's own heart. And the man who was given everything, the kingdom, the Spirit, the prophet, the second chances, would not obey, and now he hangs on the wall of the people's enemies, with his armor in their temple.

This is where I have to stop and let it land on me, because I am very good at wanting kings after my own heart. I want leaders and saviors and arrangements that fit the shape of my preference, that promise security on my terms, that look the way I think strength should look. We choose our Sauls, tall and impressive, and we are slow to learn that a throne is not kept by the qualities that won it. Saul's height did not keep him. His anointing did not keep him, because he treated it as his to spend. The crown God gives is not a possession. It is a trust, and a trust can be forfeited, and Beth-shan is what forfeiture looks like in the morning light.

**The Mercy That Remembered**

And then, at the very end, a flicker of something better. The men of Jabesh-gilead hear what the Philistines have done. Years before, Saul's first act as king had been to ride to their rescue when Nahash the Ammonite threatened to gouge out their eyes. They have not forgotten. The valiant men rise, travel all night, take down the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, bring them back, burn them, and bury the bones under a tree, and fast seven days. In the wreckage of a failed king, mercy remembers the one good thing and gives him an honorable grave. The kindness Saul once showed comes back to bury him. Even at the bottom of this story, grace finds a foothold.

We stand here with a hard lesson. The thing we demand, the king after our own liking, may be given to us, and may not be able to hold the weight we put on it. Every Saul we crown will end on some wall. There is no security in the king who looks like the nations.

But the chapter is not only an ending. It clears the ground. With Saul dead on Gilboa, the way opens for the king after God's own heart, and David's house leads to one greater than David. There is a King who was also lifted up where the people could see Him, also fastened to wood between His enemies, also stripped and mocked and pierced. But that King was not the wages of His own disobedience. He was lifted up for ours, and the throne He took up He will never lose, because death itself could not unseat Him. The crown of thorns became the crown that the grave could not remove. Saul was the king the people wanted, dead on a wall. Jesus is the King God gave, alive forever, and His kingdom has no end.

Stop crowning Sauls. There is a true King.

The throne God gives, only God keeps.
